interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: Cost-Aware Query Routing in RAG: Empirical Analysis of Retrieval Depth Tradeoffs
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) faces a fundamental three-way tension: deeper retrieval improves factual grounding but inflates token costs and end-to-end latency. Static retrieval configurations cannot resolve this tension across heterogeneous query workloads -- simple definitional queries waste budget on unnecessary context, while complex analytical prompts are underserved by shallow retrieval. This paper introduces \emph{Cost-Aware RAG} (CA-RAG), a per-query routing framework that selects from a discrete catalog of \emph{strategy bundles} -- each coupling a retrieval depth (from retrieval-free direct inference to top-$k{=}10$ dense retrieval) with a fixed generation profile -- by maximizing a scalar utility that linearly combines an estimated quality prior with normalized penalties for predicted latency and total billed tokens. CA-RAG is implemented with FAISS-backed dense retrieval and OpenAI chat/embedding APIs, and evaluated on a 28-query benchmark spanning four bundles. The router dynamically exercises all bundles, achieving \textbf{26\% fewer billed tokens} than always-heavy retrieval and \textbf{34\% lower mean latency} than always-direct inference while maintaining equivalent answer quality. Per-query delta analysis reveals that savings are non-uniform and concentrated in simpler queries, motivating complexity-aware guardrails. Sensitivity analysis confirms that the same bundle catalog supports multiple cost-latency-quality operating points through weight adjustment alone. All results are generated directly from logged CSV artifacts for full reproducibility. CA-RAG provides a transparent, auditable foundation for cost-conscious LLM deployments.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses cost-aware query routing in RAG, a key component for building efficient LLM-based research agents for astronomy literature review and data analysis.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the problem of balancing retrieval depth, latency, and cost in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. It introduces Cost-Aware RAG (CA-RAG), a framework that dynamically selects a retrieval strategy (from no retrieval to top-10 dense retrieval) per query based on a utility score that combines estimated answer quality, latency, and token cost. For astronomy, this could enable building a research agent that efficiently queries a large corpus of papers, data catalogs, or instrument documentation without wasting compute on simple lookups while still providing deep context for complex questions. A concrete workflow would be an agent that helps analyze JWST spectra: a simple query like 'what is the redshift of GN-z11?' uses a cheap direct answer, while a complex query like 'compare the SED fitting results for little red dots across three different codes' triggers deep retrieval. The main caveat is that the router's quality prior must be calibrated to the specific domain (astronomy QA), and the benchmark used is small (28 queries), so domain-specific validation is needed.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the quality prior is learned from human annotations or heuristics, and whether it could be adapted to astronomy-specific QA datasets.
Look for the per-query delta analysis to understand which query types drive cost savings and whether those types map to common astronomy questions.
Examine the sensitivity analysis to see how the cost-latency-quality tradeoff shifts when the utility weights are tuned for a research agent use case.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Clarification in LLM Agents with Information Gain
papers.authors: Mengyi Deng , Zhiwei Li , Xin Li , Tingyu Zhu , Ying Zhao , Zhijiang Guo , Wei Wang
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents often operate under underspecified user instructions, where latent uncertainty over user intent leads to erroneous tool actions. To address this challenge, we propose a goal-oriented clarification framework that aligns clarification behavior with ambiguity resolution. Central to our approach is the Information Gain Reward, a metric that quantifies the utility of clarification questions by measuring the Bayesian belief update towards the ground-truth goal induced by the clarification exchange. We train the clarifier (LLM) using this reward to optimize for high information gain, ensuring that clarifications effectively reduce uncertainty and improve task completion within the agent-tool-user environment. We validate our framework within a clarification-enhanced $\tau$-Bench environment, conducting cross-agent evaluations across five heterogeneous backbones. Empirical results demonstrate that our method consistently improves the success rate by 3.7\% over the no-clarification baseline, while adding only 0.3 total interaction steps on average.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses uncertainty quantification and goal-oriented clarification in LLM agents, which is highly relevant to building reliable research agents for astronomy workflows.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the problem of LLM agents making erroneous tool actions when user instructions are underspecified due to latent uncertainty over intent. The core idea is a goal-oriented clarification framework that uses an Information Gain Reward metric, which quantifies how much a clarification question reduces uncertainty about the true goal by measuring Bayesian belief updates. For astronomy, this could help build agents that ask clarifying questions when a researcher gives vague instructions for data analysis or literature search, reducing errors in automated workflows. A concrete workflow would be an agent that, when asked to 'find interesting high-redshift galaxies,' asks clarifying questions about redshift range, selection criteria, or data source before querying a catalog. A key caveat is that the framework was validated in a simplified tool-use environment (τ-Bench) and may need adaptation to handle the complexity of astronomical databases and analysis tools.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the Information Gain Reward is computed using a tractable approximation or exact Bayesian inference, and whether it scales to large action spaces.
Look for details on how the clarifier is trained and whether the reward model requires a separate dataset of user intents.
Examine the cross-agent evaluation results to see if performance gains hold across different LLM backbones relevant to astronomy (e.g., open-source models).

papers.title: APIC: Amortized Physics-Informed Calibration using Neural Processes
papers.authors: Aishwarya Venkataramanan , Sai Karthikeya Vemuri , Joachim Denzler
papers.abstract: Physics models are inherently imperfect due to misspecified or missing mechanisms, resulting in systematic discrepancies between model predictions and real-world observations. The Kennedy-O'Hagan (KOH) framework addresses this issue through explicit discrepancy modeling. However, its non-amortized, per-instance formulation limits scalability across families of related systems. We introduce Amortized Physics-Informed Calibration (APIC), a population-level extension of KOH that leverages Neural Processes to perform scalable Bayesian inference across realizations. Our framework employs a two-branch latent architecture to disentangle instance-specific physical parameters from shared, state-dependent structural discrepancies. By integrating differentiable physics into an amortized inference backbone, APIC enables rapid calibration of unseen realizations from sparse observations while quantifying uncertainty. Experiments on the damped spring oscillator, the Lotka-Volterra system, and the advection-diffusion PDE with misspecified physics demonstrate improved parameter recovery and consistent identification of the systemic discrepancy structure compared to other calibration approaches.
papers.Reasons for match: Amortized physics-informed calibration directly addresses systematic discrepancies between models and observations, a core problem in astrophysics (e.g., SED fitting, galaxy formation models).
papers.Short digest: This paper proposes a method to calibrate physics models by learning systematic discrepancies across many related systems. The main idea uses Neural Processes for amortized Bayesian inference, disentangling physical parameters from shared structural errors. For astronomy, this could calibrate galaxy formation simulations against observations, or improve SED fitting by learning systematic biases in stellar population models. The method is demonstrated on ODEs and PDEs, not astrophysical models. A prerequisite is a differentiable physics simulator or a surrogate model.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method scales to high-dimensional parameter spaces (e.g., >100 parameters).
Look for experiments on real-world data with known systematic errors, not just synthetic.

papers.title: A Fast Methane Detection Pipeline on Board Satellites Based on Mag1c-SAS and LinkNet
papers.authors: Jonáš Herec , Vít Růžička , Rado Pitoňák , Jan Sedmidubsky
papers.abstract: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and detecting leaks early via hyperspectral satellite imagery can help climate change mitigation efforts. Meanwhile, many existing hyperspectral missions only capture areas manually targeted by operators, thus missing potential events of interest. To overcome slow downlink rates cost-effectively, onboard detection is a viable solution. However, traditional methane detection methods are too computationally demanding for resource-limited onboard hardware. This work accelerates methane detection by focusing on efficient, low-power algorithms. In particular, we test fast target detection ACE and CEM methods that have not been previously used for methane detection and propose Mag1c-SAS -- a significantly faster variant of the current state-of-the-art Mag1c algorithm. To explore their detection potential, we integrate them with a machine learning model based on U-Net and LinkNet. We evaluate our methods on the STARCOP dataset and a novel EMIT-MSeg dataset, which we introduce and open-source alongside a high-quality annotation strategy. The proposed Mag1c-SAS approach proves highly effective by operating ~80x faster than the original Mag1c approach, providing a visually similar, but noisier result. When additionally paired with the lightweight LinkNet approach, it effectively reduces noise, achieving AUPRC score improvements of over 30 pp on EMIT-MSeg compared to the baseline Mag1c approach, and an F1 score on STARCOP ~4 pp higher. We evaluate two novel band selection strategies and confirm the system's onboard viability through hardware profiling, demonstrating marginal power consumption and efficient CPU/RAM utilization. We release the final system in a user-friendly and lightweight PyPI library at: this https URL , alongside all experimental code, models, and data at: this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: Directly relevant: fast methane detection on satellites using hyperspectral imagery, with methods transferable to astronomical source detection and onboard processing.
papers.Short digest: This paper aims to enable fast methane detection from hyperspectral satellite imagery onboard resource-limited hardware, which is crucial for timely climate action. It accelerates the Mag1c algorithm (Mag1c-SAS, ~80x faster) and pairs it with a lightweight LinkNet neural network to reduce noise. The methods are evaluated on real satellite data and shown to be viable for onboard processing with low power consumption. For astronomy, the same approach could be applied to onboard detection of transient events (e.g., supernovae, GRB afterglows) in survey data from missions like Roman or Euclid, or to real-time spectral feature detection. The caveat is that the method is tuned for methane absorption features, so adaptation to astronomical spectral lines would require retraining on appropriate data.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the band selection strategies and whether they can be adapted for astronomical spectral lines
Look at the hardware profiling results to assess feasibility for space-based platforms
Examine the LinkNet architecture and whether it can be replaced with a model trained on astronomical data
Review the EMIT-MSeg dataset annotation strategy for potential adaptation to astronomical segmentation tasks

papers.title: Agent libOS: A Library-OS-Inspired Runtime for Long-Running, Capability-Controlled LLM Agents
papers.subjects: Operating Systems (cs.OS) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR)
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from request-response assistants into long-running software actors: they maintain state across model calls, fork subtasks, wait for external events, request human authority, generate tools, and perform side effects that must be resumed and audited. This paper presents Agent libOS, a library-OS-inspired runtime substrate for LLM agents. Agent libOS runs above a conventional host operating system; it does not implement hardware drivers, kernel-mode isolation, or a POSIX-compatible operating system. Instead, it treats an agent as an AgentProcess: a schedulable execution subject with process identity, parent-child lineage, lifecycle state, a tool table derived from an AgentImage, typed Object Memory, explicit capabilities, human queues, checkpoints, events, and audit records. Its central design rule is tools are libc-like wrappers; runtime primitives are the authority boundary. Filesystem access, object access, sleeps, human approval, JIT tool registration, and external side effects are checked at primitive boundaries under explicit capabilities and policy. We describe the design, threat model, Python prototype, and safety-oriented evaluation. The current prototype implements async scheduling, namespace-local Object Memory, runtime-integrated human approval, one-shot permission grants, per-process working directories, shell and image-registration primitives, Deno/TypeScript JIT tools over a libOS syscall broker, filesystem/object bridge tools, an injectable Resource Provider Substrate, deterministic demos, real-model smoke scripts, and 123 regression tests at the time of writing. Rather than improving planner accuracy, Agent libOS demonstrates a runtime substrate in which long-running LLM agents can be scheduled, authorized, resumed, and audited without treating tool dispatch as the trust boundary.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper designs a runtime system for long-running, capability-controlled LLM agents, which is directly relevant to building reliable research agents for automated scientific discovery.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks how to build a runtime system for LLM agents that can maintain state across model calls, fork subtasks, wait for events, and be safely resumed and audited. It introduces Agent libOS, which treats an agent as an AgentProcess with identity, lifecycle, typed memory, explicit capabilities, and audit records. For astronomy, this could provide the infrastructure for a research agent that runs long-lived data analysis workflows, e.g., a multi-step SED fitting pipeline that queries databases, runs models, and waits for human approval. The key design principle is that tools are like libc wrappers and runtime primitives enforce the authority boundary, which is crucial for safe autonomous operation. A major caveat is that the current prototype is Python-based and has 123 regression tests, but it has not been tested on astronomical workflows; adapting it would require wrapping astronomical tools and defining appropriate capability policies.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the AgentProcess model supports checkpointing and resumption of long-running scientific computations.
Look for details on the capability system: can it enforce fine-grained permissions for astronomical database access or pipeline execution?
Assess the Object Memory: can it store and retrieve astronomical data products (images, spectra, catalogs)?
Check whether the runtime supports integration with existing astronomical software (astropy, JWST pipeline, etc.) via the tool system.
